meta.title: Connectomes for bet365
meta.summary: A standalone 8-12 minute film for technical bet365 colleagues explaining what connectomes are, how bet36fly uses a fruit-fly circuit with engineered sports inputs, and why emerging fly, zebrafish, and mammalian maps matter for engineers. The narration introduces biological terms inline and credits Google Research with HHMI Janelia, the University of Cambridge, and the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology.
meta.voice_instructions: Warm, gentle, conversational American English with natural pauses and even emphasis.
meta.production_status: Complete: Claude-approved narration, actual factory render, media and visual checks passed

scenes.title: Animal Architecture
scenes.narration: What could you build with a neural network whose architecture came from an animal?
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing editorial still: fruit fly as an unlikely engineering colleague, warm scientific composition, opening question mood, no added on-screen text required.

scenes.title: The Starting Point
scenes.narration: A connectome gives you that starting point: a map of an animal's neurons and the connections between them. At the sports betting company bet three sixty-five, we're exploring how circuitry shaped by an animal's life responds to a completely different kind of information. Sports gives us a familiar problem to bring to that unfamiliar architecture.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing credited title still for bet36fly and the male fruit fly nervous system, with Google Research and scientific collaborators visually prominent.

scenes.title: Cells and Synapses
scenes.narration: A biological neuron is a cell with branches that reach toward other cells. Where they make contact, a junction called a synapse carries signals between them. Researchers trace those cells and contacts through real tissue to build the map.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing still showing the reconstructed specimen and tissue-tracing problem, suitable for explaining neurons, branches, and synapses.

scenes.title: Scale of the Map
scenes.narration: Connectomes come in different sizes: some cover a single circuit, some a region, some a whole brain. The one behind this project covers a male fruit fly's brain together with its ventral nerve cord, the bundle of nervous tissue running down into its body — roughly a hundred and sixty-seven thousand neurons, in a volume smaller than a sesame seed.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing architecture still with address-book feeling, showing the male fly brain and ventral nerve cord as a mapped biological network.

scenes.title: Physical Reconstruction
scenes.narration: Recovering a map like that is slow physical work. The tissue is preserved and sliced far thinner than a wavelength of light, and every slice goes under an electron microscope. What comes back is a stack of tens of thousands of images in which a neuron appears only as a cross-section, a smudge that has to be matched to the smudge above it and the smudge below it, through every branch and every turn, past thousands of neighboring cells doing the same thing.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing electron-microscopy reconstruction still, conveying thin slices, image stacks, and tracing through crowded biological tissue.

scenes.title: Research Credit
scenes.narration: Google Research built the machine-learning systems that draft those tracings, working with HHMI Janelia, the University of Cambridge, and the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, whose scientists proofread and corrected the result. The imaging and tracing methods behind it were developed over decades. This particular resource went public in June twenty twenty-six, and the paper followed in September.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing still centered on Google Research and collaborators, with institutional collaboration and proofreading of neural tracings as the visual subject.

scenes.title: Graph With Structure
scenes.narration: What an engineer downloads at the end of all that is a graph. Neurons are the nodes, connections are the edges, and each edge carries the number of synaptic contacts the two cells make with each other. The graph arrives with structure already in it: dedicated routes for vision, for smell, for driving legs and wings, for holding onto something that happened a moment ago. Nobody drew that layout on a whiteboard. It is there because it kept flies alive.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing network-architecture still showing inherited biological routes for vision, smell, movement, and memory rather than a hand-designed neural network.

scenes.title: Equations for Activity
scenes.narration: To make that graph respond, we give its neurons equations that describe their behavior: how much voltage builds in a modeled neuron as inputs arrive, how much charge crosses a synapse, when the cell fires, and how quickly it settles afterward.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing simulator still showing wiring plus dynamics, emphasizing equations that make the anatomical map unfold in time.

scenes.title: Spiking Timing
scenes.narration: Those equations come out of the experimental literature — fly neurons have been recorded from for decades, and published spiking models of fly circuits are already there to work from. So the wiring comes out of the animal, the timing comes out of a simulator, and running the thing means running both.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing spiking-neuron still, with incoming signals, voltage buildup, pulse firing, and relaxation over simulated time.

scenes.title: No Baseball Input
scenes.narration: Which brings us to the awkward part. A fruit fly's nervous system has no input for baseball. It has inputs for light, for odor molecules, for the taste of something sweet and the taste of something bitter, for the position of its own legs. We named our project bet three sixty fly after the animal supplying the wiring. Our first engineering problem is the adapter.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing bet365 adapter still, showing baseball information approaching a fly sensory system that was built for light, odor, taste, and body position.

scenes.title: Taste Pathways
scenes.narration: We use the taste pathways. The pregame numbers for a team — recent form, the starting pitcher, the ordinary inputs any baseball model takes — become patterns of stimulation on the food-attraction and food-avoidance pathways, an engineered version of putting something sweet or something bitter in front of the animal.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing food-related stimulation still, showing engineered sweet and bitter pathways as the interface between baseball pregame information and the modeled fly circuit.

scenes.title: Two Teams
scenes.narration: Each team's stimulus uses only information available before the game. Both teams follow the same encoding rules and are presented separately. Both can taste good; the encoding preserves their individual qualities.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing two-opportunities still, showing home and away teams encoded separately under identical rules with appetitive patterns possible for both.

scenes.title: Circuit Response
scenes.narration: Then you run it and watch. Activity spreads from the taste inputs through whatever the wiring allows, settles, and leaves a pattern across a set of neurons we chose in advance. That pattern is what we read out, and a small external model, trained on past seasons, turns the two patterns into a prediction.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing readout still, showing two sensory inputs flowing through an anatomically structured circuit to selected neurons and an external prediction head.

scenes.title: Representation Head
scenes.narration: If you work with embeddings, the shape will be familiar: something goes in, a representation comes out of the middle, and an output layer reads the representation. We designed the input adapter and the readout. The connections inside the circuit come from the measured anatomy, and the simulator follows activity through those connections over time.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing representation still, suitable for an embedding-style input, middle representation, and external readout explanation.

scenes.title: Season Test
scenes.narration: Sports gives us a way to test this chain against outcomes we can check. For our first full-season test, we fixed the model before giving it the twenty twenty-three Major League Baseball games. Across more than twenty-four hundred games, it called about fifty-six percent correctly, level with a conventional model given the same pregame information. We are still investigating which features of the fly's wiring contribute useful capabilities.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing season-through-the-circuit still, showing 2023 baseball games passing through the frozen pipeline with the exact result context preserved.

scenes.title: Named Cells
scenes.narration: The circuit gives that investigation a physical reference: named cells and the connections measured between them. One experiment we can design is to quiet a selected pathway, present the same matchup again, and compare the response.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing pathway-intervention still, showing a named neural route being silenced while the same matchup input is replayed.

scenes.title: Altered Wiring
scenes.narration: Comparing the intact circuit with altered wiring is how we can test which parts of the anatomy contribute to the representation.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing circuit-comparison still, emphasizing intact versus altered wiring and response comparison.

scenes.title: Experience Changes
scenes.narration: We can also let experience change the connections. A living fly carries the previous encounter into the next one. A fly that finds food while a particular smell is in the air will treat that smell differently the next time it drifts past.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing kitchen-fly memory still, showing yesterday's experience affecting today's sensory response.

scenes.title: Mushroom Body
scenes.narration: The structure behind that is called the mushroom body, where sensory signals meet a teaching signal carried by dopamine. We implemented an association experiment in a separate version of our simulator: pair a cue with the teaching signal, wait, then present the cue on its own, and the circuit answers it differently than it did before.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing mushroom-body learning still, showing sensory cue patterns meeting a dopamine teaching signal in the fly learning circuit.

scenes.title: Cue Specificity
scenes.narration: The change stays specific to the cue that was trained, and it reverses when the teaching signal reverses. This lets us study a representation that changes with experience, alongside the fixed responses used in the season test.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing teaching-a-cue still, showing cue-specific association, reversal with teaching signal reversal, and a changed later response.

scenes.title: Different Environment
scenes.narration: Once you have an adapter into the circuit, you can give it a different environment. A developer connected the same released wiring to Doom, the first-person shooter, in a project called DOOMFLY. Game frames go in as input, the code path runs through the retained connectome graph, and a fixed set of outputs is mapped onto moving and shooting.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing Doom still, showing game frames as neural input and fixed outputs mapped to movement and firing.

scenes.title: Scripted or Neural
scenes.narration: The screen alone can hide how a demo works. A browser can also show a convincing fly animation using JavaScript and entirely scripted movement. When you watch a fly demo online, look for what controls its next action. In DOOMFLY, you can open the repository and follow a game frame through the neural model to a keypress.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing controls-and-code still, showing the distinction between scripted browser animation and an inspectable route through a neural model to action.

scenes.title: Input Action Loop
scenes.narration: In Doom, each action changes the next game frame. Turning alters the view; moving brings something closer. The circuit's outputs become part of its next input.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing richer-environment still, showing a closed loop where action changes the next sensory frame.

scenes.title: Vision and Body
scenes.narration: Giving that loop the sensory detail and physical consequences of an animal's world is a larger undertaking. FlyVis develops the visual side: researchers constrain a model with measured fly connectivity, train it on visual tasks, and compare its responses with recordings from real cells.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing research-lineage still for FlyVis and FlyBody, connecting measured visual connectivity, recordings, physics, and body control.

scenes.title: Future Controller
scenes.narration: FlyBody supplies a body in a physics engine, with reinforcement-learning controllers for walking and flight. It provides a way to test the consequences of a controller's outputs, down to whether the fly keeps its feet on the ground.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing body-to-inhabit still, showing a simulated fly body with walking and flight control consequences.

scenes.title: Two Timescales
scenes.narration: The reason all of this is arriving at once is that two very different timescales met. The imaging, the tracing, the proofreading — that is decades of method and years of work on this one specimen, released in June. The experiments built on top of it are weeks old.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing weeks-and-years still, contrasting long reconstruction work with recent experimental pipelines.

scenes.title: Agents Speed the Work
scenes.narration: Reading into an unfamiliar literature, writing an adapter, getting somebody else's research code to run used to be the slow parts, and coding agents built on large language models have made them cheap enough that a small team can cross from neuroscience to a running pipeline in days.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing pace-change still, showing connectomics releases and LLM coding agents making cross-field engineering faster.

scenes.title: Better Maps
scenes.narration: And the maps keep improving. A larval zebrafish is transparent, which means you can point a microscope at a living one and watch neurons light up across most of its brain while the animal behaves.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing zebrafish still, showing transparent larval zebrafish with brain activity visible during behavior.

scenes.title: Wiring With Activity
scenes.narration: Google Research is working toward pairing a zebrafish wiring map with activity recorded from the same specimen. The associated activity dataset already covers more than seventy thousand neurons. You could run your equations on the measured wiring, compare the result with what those same neurons did, and tighten the model where the two disagree. The recordings would give the simulator a detailed target from the animal it represents.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing wiring-meets-activity still, showing Fish2 and ZAPBench-style pairing of wiring with activity from the same specimen.

scenes.title: Measured Targets
scenes.narration: The same approach is reaching mammalian circuits. The MICrONS project reconstructed a block of mouse visual cortex, the brain tissue that processes vision, containing roughly half a billion synaptic contacts alongside activity recordings.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing mammalian-tissue still, showing mouse visual cortex reconstruction with synapses and linked activity recordings.

scenes.title: Mammalian Programs
scenes.narration: Larger mapping programs are underway, bringing increasingly rich circuits within reach of this kind of experiment.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing tools-that-carry-forward still, showing engineering methods extending from fly circuits toward larger measured biological architectures.

scenes.title: What We Can Do
scenes.narration: We started with a network architecture that came from an animal. We can now give part of that network an unfamiliar input, measure the response, and change a pathway to see what it contributes.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing choose-a-problem still, showing an environment entering a biological circuit and response measurements becoming inspectable.

scenes.title: The Fly Today
scenes.narration: The fly lets us begin doing that work today. As maps of fish and mammalian brains develop, engineers will have more biological architectures to build around, with recordings that show how those circuits worked in the living animal.
scenes.visual_prompt: Existing final outlook still, returning from the kitchen fly to biological architectures and future measured circuits.
